items.item: Every value has exactly one owner at a time, and that owner (a binding, a field, a container slot, a closure environment) is the single party responsible for running its destructor when it goes out of scope.

at.deep: What a move is, as the Reference states it

items.item: A move copies only the inline bytes (for String: pointer, length, capacity) and statically invalidates the source, so the heap buffer is never duplicated and never freed twice; Rust never inserts an implicit deep copy, so any implicit copy is cheap by construction.

items.item: Invalidation is a compile-time property of the place, not a runtime state of the value: a moved-from local is deinitialized, every read is rejected until it is assigned again, and reassigning a `let mut` binding after a move is legal and revives it.

items.item: Loops are where moves bite: `for x in v` desugars to `IntoIterator::into_iter(v)` and consumes `v` (iterate `&v` or `&mut v` to borrow), and moving a non-Copy outer variable inside a loop body is rejected because the next iteration would read a deinitialized place, unless the body reassigns it or breaks.

items.item: `Copy` means the implicit duplicate is a plain bitwise copy that cannot run user code and leaves the source usable; `Clone` is an explicit, possibly expensive call to arbitrary code, so the presence or absence of `.clone()` shows the reader where the cost is.

items.item: The compiler’s E0382 help text ("consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable") is a suggestion, not a fix; an expert first asks whether the callee should borrow (`&T`), whether the caller still needs the value, or whether ownership should be handed back by return.

A `.clone()` call does not always mean a deep copy: `Rc::clone` and `Arc::clone` only bump a reference count, which is why the convention `Rc::clone(&a)` is used to make shared-ownership handles visibly different from data copies.

items.item: `Copy` and `Drop` are mutually exclusive (E0184): a type that owns a resource beyond its own bytes cannot be duplicated bitwise, so any type with a destructor, or any field with one, always has move semantics.

items.item: Shared references `&T` are `Copy` whatever `T` is, but `&mut T` is never `Copy`, because copying it would create two aliasing mutable references; this is why passing a `&mut` moves it (the reborrowing that hides this is covered with borrowing).

items.item: Signatures are ownership contracts that callers can read without opening the body: a `T` or `self` parameter consumes the argument, `&T`/`&self` borrows it, `&mut T`/`&mut self` borrows it exclusively, and returning `T` hands ownership back; a by-value `self` is the tool for "after this call the old value must not be used" (builders, `into_*`, state transitions).

`&mut T` in a signature promises exclusivity, not just mutability: while it is live no other reference to the value may exist, which is what lets the callee mutate without the defensive copying or locking a C++ or Java programmer would add.

E0382 (use of moved value) has three labelled spans to read in order: where the value was moved, why it moved (its type is not `Copy`), and the later use; the fix depends on which of those three you change (borrow at the move site, derive Copy/Clone, or reorder or reassign before the use).

E0505 (move out while borrowed) means a live borrow outlives the point where ownership leaves; because borrows end at their last use, the usual fix is to move the last use of the reference before the move, not to clone.

items.item: Rust has no move constructor: a move is always a byte copy with no user hook, and a value’s address can change at any move, so code must never rely on a value staying at a stable address unless it is pinned.

at.deep: A move is a bit copy, and addresses change

items.item: Unlike C++ `std::move`, which is only a cast that hands the object to a user-written move constructor and leaves a moved-from object that is still destroyed and must stay valid, a Rust move ends the source binding statically, runs no destructor on it, and needs no "null out the source" code.

at.deep: C++, Go, Java and Python, precisely

items.item: Conditional moves (moving in one branch only) are legal: when the compiler cannot know statically whether a value is still owned at scope end, it keeps a hidden drop flag on the stack and checks it at run time to decide whether to drop.

at.topic: RAII, drop order, and leak safety

items.item: Closures are owners too: `move` makes a closure capture by value (needed for `thread::spawn` and returned closures), but which `Fn` trait it implements depends on what the body does with the captures; only a body that moves a capture out is limited to `FnOnce`, and moving out of a capture in an `Fn`/`FnMut` closure is E0507.

items.item: Patterns move: `match opt { Some(s) => .. }` or `let (a, b) = pair;` moves non-Copy parts out of the scrutinee and leaves it unusable, while `_` binds nothing and moves nothing, and matching on `&opt` switches the default binding mode to `ref` so nothing moves.

items.item: Because any move may relocate a value, a self-referential value would leave dangling internal pointers if moved; safe Rust stops this by forbidding moves while a borrow is live, and `Pin` exists for the cases (async futures) where that is not enough.
